Remarkably, the treatment preserved brain function without removing Alzheimer’s-associated plaques, suggesting a completely different way to combat cognitive decline.

title: The narwhal’s legendary “unicorn horn” holds a remarkable engineering secret
description: The narwhal’s iconic spiral tusk, once prized in Europe as the horn of a mythical unicorn, conceals an extraordinary feat of natural engineering. Using advanced X-ray technology, an international team of scientists discovered that the tusk contains two intertwined microscopic spirals that twist in opposite directions.

title: Scientists turn one of the world’s hardest-to-recycle plastics into high-performance lubricating oil
description: Virginia Tech scientists have discovered how to transform one of the world's hardest-to-recycle plastics into a valuable ingredient for high-performance engine oil. Their innovative process converts discarded PVC into a useful lubricant material in just three hours. The breakthrough could turn a major source of plastic pollution into a valuable industrial resource while making lubricant production more sustainable.

title: Scientists discover a surprising twist in how the body burns calories
description: Researchers have discovered that a drug can significantly increase the body's energy expenditure without clearly activating calorie-burning brown fat. The unexpected finding reveals a new challenge in developing obesity treatments that harness the body's natural fat-burning machinery.

title: Alzheimer’s breakthrough exposes a hidden flaw in the brain’s cleanup system
description: Scientists have identified a gene that helps the brain’s immune cells contain harmful plaques linked to Alzheimer’s, potentially revealing a new way to fight the disease. When the gene malfunctioned in mice, toxic buildup accelerated and cognitive abilities declined, raising hopes that restoring its function could help protect the brain.

title: Too much exercise could leave your brain stuck in overdrive
description: Exercising too much without adequate recovery may disrupt brain chemistry in surprising ways. Scientists found that mice subjected to prolonged, intense training had elevated dopamine levels in a brain region linked to memory and emotions, even 48 hours after exercising. The discovery could help explain why overtrained athletes sometimes struggle with insomnia, anxiety, and persistent fatigue, although these symptoms were not directly measured.

title: Working in Cape Cod’s waters, he saw an unusual clam. It was the start of an invasion
description:

Send us your climate questions for the next Stateside guest: Bill McKibben

Shellfish harvester Ernie Eldredge is on the hunt for clams, ankle-deep in water amid a landscape that’s almost desert-like in the wake of the receding tide. He runs his rake through fine white sand again and again without hearing the faint “clink” of its tines hitting a shell.
Eldredge just shrugs and moves on to the next spot. These tidal flats, perched on the elbow of Cape Cod in Chatham, Massachusetts, are constantly changing. Recent fall winds have carried a lot more sand into the area, and Eldredge thinks the clams he was finding over the summer may have moved on.

title: This 345-million-year-old fossil had scientists fooled for decades
description: A famous 345-million-year-old fossil has turned out to be something entirely different from what scientists believed for decades. Advanced X-ray imaging revealed hidden gills and thousands of tiny teeth, exposing a primitive aquatic or amphibious creature rather than an early reptile. The discovery suggests that several adaptations associated with life on land actually evolved in animals still dependent on water.

title: DNA’s secret sunscreen may have helped life survive on early Earth
description: Scientists have uncovered a surprising reason why early life may have survived Earth's intense ultraviolet radiation: a key component of DNA appears to turn potentially destructive damage into something easier to repair. The discovery could help solve a decades-old evolutionary mystery and reveal how life endured the harsh conditions of our planet's earliest days.

title: Who was buried in Westminster Abbey's Roman coffin? A 150-year mystery may be solved
description: A mysterious skeleton discovered in a Roman sarcophagus at Westminster Abbey may finally be identified after more than 150 years. New dating evidence suggests the remains belonged to a high-ranking medieval abbot who was buried inside a centuries-old recycled Roman coffin.

title: More than a billion years of Earth's history vanished. Scientists may finally know why
description: Scientists may have finally explained why up to more than a billion years of Earth's geological history are missing from rocks around the world. New research suggests that powerful currents deep inside the planet slowly raised and lowered entire continents, allowing erosion to erase vast stretches of geological history before they were buried and preserved.

title: The Sun unleashed a monster storm. Earth may have made it worse
description: The massive solar storm that illuminated skies worldwide in May 2024 has uncovered an unexpected twist: Earth's own atmosphere may have helped make the storm so powerful. Satellite measurements revealed that roughly 85% of the charged particles fueling the disturbance originated from Earth's upper atmosphere rather than the solar wind. Scientists also detected an extraordinary 40% weakening of Earth's magnetic field high above the planet.

title: Common supplements rival antibiotics in treating severe gum disease
description: A combination of omega-3 and low-dose aspirin produced results comparable to antibiotics when used alongside standard treatment for severe gum disease, with benefits persisting long after supplementation ended. The surprising discovery could offer an alternative for some patients while reducing reliance on antibiotics.

title: Stanford scientists discover 3 hidden brain types behind ADHD and anxiety
description: An AI-powered analysis of thousands of children's brain scans has revealed three distinct brain types underlying ADHD and anxiety that do not neatly fit traditional diagnoses. These hidden biological patterns can appear before a diagnosis is made, potentially enabling earlier detection and more effective, personalized treatments.

title: Peppermint oil significantly lowers blood pressure in just 20 days
description: Peppermint oil may have a surprisingly powerful effect on blood pressure. In a randomized study of 40 adults, researchers found that taking small doses twice daily for 20 days lowered systolic blood pressure by an average of 8.5 mmHg. Those receiving a placebo experienced no significant improvement. The discovery points to a promising, low-cost natural approach to managing mildly elevated blood pressure.

title: Scientists discover a hidden gut defense that could prevent colon cancer
description: A common antibody in the gut may be a powerful natural defense against colon cancer, with researchers finding that mice lacking it developed more than twice as many tumors. Restoring the antibody eliminated the increased risk, revealing a promising new avenue for preventing cancer before it starts.

title: For decades, scientists may have misunderstood how brain cells work
description: A major new study challenges a long-standing assumption about how the brain works, revealing that most neurons are versatile multitaskers rather than highly specialized workers. By analyzing recordings from 43 regions of the mouse brain, researchers discovered that although some neurons are dedicated to specific functions, most respond to a wide variety of information in remarkably distinct ways.

With an estimated mass only three times that of the Moon, it may be a 13-billion-year-old cosmic relic that offers new clues to the mystery of dark matter.

title: The US army just detonated a poison bomb over Iowa | Steven Donziger
description:
The shocking situation in Iowa is a metaphor for much of what is wrong with the United States
There’s no way to hide it: the US government just deliberately detonated a poison bomb of lead azide over the state of Iowa when a totally safe alternative was available.
The problem in Iowa was relatively simple to solve. The army for decades had stored lead underground at a munitions facility. As far back as 2009, the government knew the lead was deteriorating and might blow up on its own. But it procrastinated. Finally, in March, the army hired a Georgia-based company to use a chemical spray to neutralize the lead, creating a non-hazardous byproduct that can be disposed of in landfills.
Steven Donziger is a US-based human rights and environmental lawyer and the author of Donziger On Justice on Substack
 Continue reading...

title: Suit alleges Louisiana land deal between SpaceX and ExxonMobil violates open meetings law
description:
Suit says parish board was manipulated to allow deal to go through and settlement agreement hidden from public
After ending a lawsuit over ExxonMobil’s damage to wetlands, Louisiana officials moved quickly to approve a deal giving SpaceX access to 125,000 acres (50,600 hectares) of marsh formerly owned by the oil company. A new lawsuit now alleges they did so in violation of the state’s open meetings law.
The lawsuit, filed by three south-central Louisiana residents, follows state and Vermilion parish officials’ approval of what is estimated to be a record $27.5bn tax incentive package for SpaceX’s Starbase Louisiana project, announced over the summer. The officials violated the state’s open meetings law eight times while facilitating the agreement in attempts to “keep the public in the dark about what they are doing for SpaceX”, the lawsuit alleges.
 Continue reading...

title: Scientists discover mysterious lakes more than a mile beneath the Red Sea
description: More than a mile beneath the surface of the Red Sea, scientists have discovered rare underwater lakes that could reveal secrets about Earth's ancient oceans and the possibility of alien life. Known as brine pools, these extremely salty, oxygen-free environments are surprisingly teeming with microbial life, challenging our understanding of where living organisms can survive.

title: Earth's core may be leaking a 4.5-billion-year-old secret
description: Scientists have discovered an unusual carbon signature in Hawaiian volcanic rocks that suggests some of Earth's carbon originated in ancient meteorites and later escaped from deep within the planet's core. The discovery raises an astonishing possibility: Carbon essential to life may have traveled from space to Earth's depths before emerging through volcanoes billions of years later.

title: This tiny spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome 50% larger than a human’s
description: A tiny California trapdoor spider named after Stephen Colbert has a genome roughly 50% larger than a human's, despite being only about the size of a quarter. Scientists discovered that its enormous genome contains 4.6 billion DNA base pairs and 52 chromosomes, revealing surprising clues about spider evolution.

title: Archaeologists reveal a powerful Iron Age king may have been a woman
description: Archaeologists have uncovered evidence that Verica, the Iron Age ruler whose exile helped trigger Rome’s invasion of Britain in AD 43, was actually a woman. The discovery challenges centuries of historical assumptions and suggests that a largely forgotten female leader may have changed the course of British history.

title: Mysterious new viruses reveal a missing link in evolution
description: Scientists have discovered previously unknown viruses that could help explain how some of life’s earliest biological structures evolved. The surprising findings challenge a longstanding evolutionary theory and suggest that viruses may have hidden capabilities far beyond simply infecting cells.

title: 125,000 years ago, hippos roamed what is now the vast Arabian Desert
description: A remarkable 125,000-year-old discovery in Saudi Arabia reveals that early humans once thrived beside enormous lakes filled with wildlife in what is now a vast desert. Thousands of stone tools and ancient plant remains suggest these prehistoric people used sophisticated hunting techniques, potentially including weapons enhanced with poisonous plant compounds.

title: A new treasure map reveals where Earth's lost prehistoric life may be hiding
description: A sweeping analysis of 540 million years of marine fossils has revealed surprising gaps in our understanding of Earth's ancient life. Scientists discovered that some of the greatest opportunities for finding previously unknown species lie in relatively recent geological periods, rather than the distant past. By mapping unexplored fossil-rich regions around the world, researchers have created a powerful tool to guide future excavations.

title: Superheated magma could fuel towering lava fountains
description: Why do some volcanoes erupt with spectacular lava fountains while others release lava more quietly? Scientists have discovered that a hidden effect of extreme heat inside magma may help explain the difference. Experiments revealed that superheated magma can delay crystal formation for more than eight hours, compared with just 20 minutes in magma that has not been superheated.

title: Hidden climate superpower: Why some ocean “snow” carries six times more carbon
description: Scientists have discovered that the stickiness of underwater “marine snow” plays a surprisingly important role in how much carbon reaches the deep ocean. Gooier particles resist bacterial breakdown and can transport more than six times as much carbon to the depths, revealing an unexpected connection between ocean slime and Earth's climate.

title: A fat-burning molecule has an unexpected benefit for your muscles
description: Researchers have discovered that a naturally occurring molecule released during exercise helps muscles become stronger, resist fatigue, and withstand damage. The molecule, already available as a dietary supplement, could open new avenues for treating muscle deterioration associated with type 2 diabetes.

title: This dietary supplement may have an unexpected benefit for the brain
description: A naturally derived dietary supplement called urolithin A may help the brain get more oxygen and nutrients when it needs them most. In a randomized clinical trial involving 50 middle-aged adults with obesity, researchers found that taking the supplement daily for four weeks increased blood flow to the brain during a challenging memory task, particularly in a region involved in working memory.

title: A tiny injectable sensor could change how millions of people monitor blood sugar
description: Texas A&M researchers have discovered a way to dramatically reduce the cost of a key component in an experimental injectable glucose sensor without sacrificing performance. The technology uses fluorescent light to measure glucose levels from beneath the skin.

title: Scientists discover a new type of depression that common antidepressants struggle to treat
description: Researchers have discovered a new subtype of depression that may affect nearly one in four people with severe, recurrent, or persistent depression. Known as "circadian depression," it is linked to the body's internal clock and is associated with night owl tendencies, excessive sleep, persistent exhaustion, and more severe symptoms. Traditional antidepressants often work less effectively for these individuals, potentially explaining why some people struggle to find relief.

title: Mice slept 70% less after scientists switched off these brain cells
description: Scientists have discovered brain cells that actively generate the irresistible urge to sleep, and shutting them down allowed mice to sleep 70% less than normal. Remarkably, many of the animals avoided the severe behavioral consequences of sleep deprivation, raising intriguing possibilities for future sleep research.

title: Scientists identify two ages when children may be most vulnerable to screen time
description: Scientists have identified two potentially critical periods when screen time may be especially detrimental to children's learning and memory: infancy and the start of formal schooling. Greater screen exposure during these developmental windows was linked to poorer academic performance and weaker working memory years later.

title: What is a thought made of? Why human consciousness may be beyond AI’s reach
description: A new theory suggests that the brain may chemically encode and retrieve memories rather than relying solely on electrical signals. Researchers propose that interactions between brain cells and their molecular surroundings could help explain the intimate connection between memory, emotion, and thought. Their findings challenge the assumption that increasingly powerful computers could eventually develop human-like consciousness.

title: AI may not work like the human brain after all, scientists discover
description: AI may not think like the human brain after all, according to a striking new discovery that challenges how scientists understand artificial intelligence. Researchers found that even AI models that closely predict brain activity may rely on internal processes the brain doesn't use, raising important questions about their reliability in neuroscience research.

title: For better mental health, how often you exercise may matter more than how hard
description: A study of more than 10,000 college students found that exercising regularly may be more important for mental health than pushing yourself through intense or lengthy workouts. Students who exercised less frequently were more likely to experience depression and anxiety a year later, suggesting that consistency could be a key ingredient in protecting mental well-being.

title: Want your research cited in patents? Publishing open access increases your chances

How arteries keep their shape in the face of overgrowth-inducing mutations
Hundreds of thousands still without power a day after US slammed with Thanksgiving storms
description: Pennsylvania and neighbouring states remain badly affected on Friday after both coasts were lashed with wind and rain.

title: Major Thanksgiving storm brings flooding, flight delays across US
description: Almost one million customers in the US had no power on Thursday evening as storms descended on both US coasts, bringing wind gusts, heavy rain and flooding.

title: Fireball steals the show during Thanksgiving drone display in Indiana
description: The glowing object was captured on video as holiday-themed drones illuminated the night sky.

title: Physicists trap antimatter in a breakthrough that could explain why the universe exists
description: Positrons are the antimatter counterpart of an electron. Physicists trapped a positron and cooled it to temperatures near absolute zero. Positron is suspended in a wall-free trap, safely separated from ordinary matter. Team will conduct most precise comparison yet between matter and antimatter. Any difference between the electron and positron could expose cracks in the Standard Model of particle physics.

title: Physicists just sent an unblockable message through a brick wall using gravity
description: Scientists have successfully transmitted a message through a brick wall using nothing but gravity, an old elevator, and an incredibly sensitive detector. By moving a massive counterweight between two positions, researchers encoded the word "Gravity" into tiny changes in gravitational pull. Unlike Wi-Fi or radio signals, gravity passes through ordinary barriers without being blocked, offering a potentially revolutionary way to communicate.

title: A 3-million-year-old child just made human evolution far more complicated
description: A groundbreaking study of the 3-million-year-old Taung Child fossil suggests that several ancient human ancestors once thought to belong to the same species may actually represent different branches of our evolutionary family tree. The discovery challenges a century of assumptions and reveals how dramatic climate changes helped shape a surprisingly complex story of human origins.

title: Something strange is living beneath the skin of deep-sea pigs
description: Scientists have discovered a strange bacterium hiding beneath the skin of deep-sea creatures known as sea pigs, revealing an unexpected biological partnership. The microbe has an unusually tiny genome, yet more than a quarter of its DNA is devoted to making surface proteins, some of them exceptionally large. Researchers suspect it depends heavily on its host for survival, but what the sea pigs gain in return remains a mystery.

title: An ancient virus may help explain what makes the human brain different
description: A virus that infected chimpanzees millions of years ago may have helped shape one of the most important differences between humans and our closest relatives: how our brains develop. Scientists at Lund University discovered that ancient viral DNA embedded in the chimpanzee genome switches off a gene called LINC00662, which remains active in humans and appears to play an important role in early brain development.

title: Dinosaurs may have been eating seaweed 100 million years ago
description: Dinosaurs may have been snacking on seaweed and other ocean foods more than 100 million years ago, according to surprising new evidence hidden in their fossilized teeth. Researchers discovered chemical signatures suggesting that coastal dinosaurs and other prehistoric animals relied partly on nutrients originating in the sea. The findings reveal that marine resources traveled through ancient food chains, supplementing the diets of everything from plant-eating dinosaurs to predators.

title: Painting to Transform the World
description: A recent exhibition at the Louvre of the work of Jacques-Louis David presented him as an artist whose political and artistic activities were deeply intertwined.
source: The New York Review of Books
author: Colin B. Bailey

title: One Little Hummingbird Flew Over 4,000 Miles in a Record-Breaking Migration
description: Small as a sparrow and light as a sugar cube, one male rufous hummingbird traversed a record-breaking 6,526 cumulative kilometers (4,055 miles) from Alabama to Alaska in just 38 days.
author: Jess Cockerill

title: Klebsiella oxytoca bacteremia in adults compared with Klebsiella pneumoniae bacteremia: Distinct clinical characteristics, treatment challenges, and comparable clinical severity
description: Background Klebsiella oxytoca is the second most common Klebsiella species causing bloodstream infection after Klebsiella pneumoniae, yet comparative data in adults remain limited. We compared the clinical characteristics and outcomes of K. oxytoca bacteremia…
author: Haruka Watanabe Keiji Nakamura Makiko Kiyosuke Noriko Miyake Koichi Akashi Nobuyuki Shimono Yong Chong
